newsitem.title: INDIA: India RBI's sterilisation to subside, says I-Sec.
newsitem.headline: India RBI's sterilisation to subside, says I-Sec.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) may not need to sterilise excess money supply in the system in coming months as much as it had to in recent months, ICICI Securities and Finance Company (I-Sec) said on Tuesday.

It said strong capital flows forced the RBI to intervene regularly in the foreign currency market resulting in a large augmentation of rupee liquidity in the banking system and a downward pressure on interest rates.
At the same time RBI had to sterilise the impact on the domestic money market quite aggressively.
"The total amount of government securities (including seven year stock) and 364-day treasury bills issued since April 1997 has been 164.33 billion rupees," it said in a research report.
"Also, the RBI has been using short term repos to squeeze out surplus funds," it said.

"However, the amount of sterilisation being done is likely to subside over the next few months and the surplus liquidity will be absorbed by the corporate sector as industrial activity is expected to pick up by August/September," it said.
I-Sec said the net accretion to RBI's foreign currency reserves in the period from March to May has been of the order of $4.47 billion, an average of nearly $1.5 billion per month.
The rupee has been fairly strong and six month forward premiums have plummeted from 8.20 perfent to nearly 4.5 percent levels.
"The drop in forwards has been primarily because of the option of swapping dollars to invest in rupee assets is no longer attractive," the repor said.
